source.title: Missed Causes and Ambiguous Effects: Counterfactuals Pose Challenges for Interpreting Neural Networks

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses Hydra effects as an example of preemption, but does not measure self-repair or test any of the listed claim versions. Its Pythia case study concerns local causal dependencies, a related but different issue.
record.gate_note: Hydra effects and backup heads are cited as examples from prior work, not results of this study. The study's own sparse-feature-circuit case study reports local dependencies, so it is recorded under fits_no_version; it does not test self-repair.
record.test_reason: A position paper on counterfactual causality in interpretability. It cites Hydra effects and backup heads (McGrath et al., Wang et al.) as examples of preemption. Its only empirical result is a Pythia 70M sparse feature circuit retargeted to an intermediate succession feature. That result concerns non-transitive local dependencies, not compensation after ablation. It reports no rate or size of self-repair, so it tests no version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors argue that counterfactual interventions miss redundant causes (overdetermination and preemption, e.g. backup heads and Hydra effects) and that counterfactual dependence is not transitive across causal chains. They recommend keeping some local dependencies, using diverse data, and using both positive and negative interventions. They still judge counterfactual theories the most actionable for interpretability. They also note that simultaneous overdetermination is not yet attested in large language models.
record.recipe_differences: The Pythia case study uses sparse feature circuit discovery with zero ablations and an intermediate-feature target; it does not apply the layer/head self-repair method or measure compensation.
record.method_sensitivity: The case study changes the target metric from next-token negative log-probability to the negative activation of layer 3 attention feature 14579; the resulting circuit includes additional local dependencies.

fits_no_version.finding: Retargeting a sparse feature circuit in Pythia 70M to an intermediate layer-3 succession feature reveals upstream local dependencies (number detectors, then number-list and increasing-sequence detectors) absent from the output-targeted circuit.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Output-targeted causal circuits omit local upstream components that explain how intermediate representations are composed (non-transitivity of counterfactual dependence).

record.problems: The empirical case study is limited to Pythia 70M and one succession cluster. It reports no control comparison or uncertainty estimates, uses a linear approximation to indirect effects, and includes manual feature annotation. The paper notes that its discussion is not a representative sample of causal and mechanistic interpretability methods.
record.rows_left_out: No other rows: results about Hydra effects, backup heads, redundancy, and other cited studies are attributed to prior work rather than reported as results of this study.

untested.parts: All; layer-ablation compensation is cited from McGrath et al., not measured.
All; backup heads are only cited as preemption examples.
All; the paper argues mean and resample ablation are more principled than zero ablation but runs no comparison.
Argued conceptually (preemption makes single-component ablation miss causes), but no empirical test of attribution misstatement due to self-repair.

record.verdict_notes: The paper's link to V7 is purely conceptual: preemption means single ablations miss backup components. It provides no self-repair measurement, so no verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: Layer-ablation compensation and restoration of the output.
Late-MLP counterbalancing and its change under earlier ablations.
Head-level self-repair on full output distributions across models.
Prompt-level variation, average compensation, and overcorrection.
Empirical tests of backup heads, copy-suppression heads, final LayerNorm rescaling, or anti-erasure neurons.
Comparison of self-repair under on-distribution and zero ablations.
Whether self-repair causes ablation-based importance scores to misstate a component's role.

rows.subject: Pythia 70M
rows.operation_detail: Zero-ablated upstream sparse autoencoder feature activations while constructing a sparse feature circuit.
rows.measure: Sparse feature circuit for the target feature's activation; the reported result is the presence of upstream local causal chains.
rows.baseline: The original cluster circuit targeted negative log-probability of the next token.
rows.value: With the target changed to the negative activation of layer 3 attention feature 14579, the circuit included additional features and edges, including chains from number detectors through number-list and increasing-sequence detectors.
rows.note: The authors report that the expanded circuit helps explain how the succession feature is composed from lower-level features. This bears on local-dependency attribution, not on self-repair.
rows.check: The row measures which upstream features enter a circuit, not compensation after ablation, so it cannot show any self-repair version. The state 'observed' only describes the presence of circuit features, not a self-repair effect. Linking it to 'none' is correct.

relation.reason: §4 interprets Hydra effects and backup heads as preemption and explains their implications for ablation-based attribution, without independently testing self-repair.

tranche.reason: The empirical case study measures upstream dependencies of an intermediate sparse feature, not self-repair. Discussion of Hydra effects and backup heads relies on prior studies.

source_check.notes: Appendix A supports the recorded negative-log-probability baseline, although §3.1 describes it as a logit difference. Circuit discovery uses an integrated-gradients approximation with zero-ablation endpoints; it does not measure compensation.
